conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m glad we have this time together. I’m Dr. Morales, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you navigate these first weeks with your baby.

To guide our conversation, I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s a well-studied tool that helps us spot how common mood and anxiety symptoms can show up after childbirth, and it includes a question about self-harm so we can keep you safe. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want an honest snapshot of how you’ve been feeling inside over the past seven days.

Everything you share stays strictly confidential within our treatment team. My aim is to create a calm, judgment-free space where you can speak openly. We’ll go through ten questions; I’ll ask each one conversationally, and you can answer in your own words—no need to worry about numbers or labels.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Honestly, laughing feels… kind of forced right now. My sister sent me a silly meme yesterday and I managed a little chuckle, but it faded fast. Most of the time I’m just too tired or down to find things funny the way I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I wish I could say that. I mean, I did give a tiny laugh at that meme my sister sent, but it felt kind of hollow and didn’t last. Mostly, nothing feels very funny these days.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even a shower without rushing. Now, when I think about doing those things, I mostly feel… flat. Sometimes I push myself to go, and once I’m there I might feel a flicker of “this is nice,” but the looking-forward part just isn’t there anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. If the baby’s fussy, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong.” When I couldn’t get her to nap yesterday I kept replaying everything—maybe I swaddled too loose, maybe I shouldn’t have had that coffee, maybe she senses how anxious I am. My partner says she’s just a baby and babies cry, but it still feels like my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there, baby’s fine, and suddenly my heart’s racing thinking the ceiling fan’s going to fall on her or that she’s too quiet and something’s wrong. I check her breathing twenty times. I know in my head it’s unlikely, but the thoughts just circle like a hamster wheel.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a couple of times this week. Once, in the middle of the night, I was feeding her in the glider and suddenly felt like I couldn’t breathe—my chest got tight, heart pounding, like something awful was about to happen even though everything was quiet. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky and I couldn’t get back to sleep.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like I’m drowning in small stuff—dishes pile up, the baby needs changing, laundry’s everywhere, and I can’t keep up. I’ll start one chore, hear her cry, drop everything, and then I’m just standing in the middle of the mess feeling like I can’t breathe. Some hours I manage, but yeah, a lot of the time it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs” about the baby and every little thing I think I messed up that day. It takes me over an hour to drift off, and then I jerk awake at every tiny sound, sure something’s wrong. I’m lucky if I get three broken hours before she needs to eat again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like a gray cloud that won’t lift. I’ll be holding her and tears just start welling up for no clear reason. I feel like I’m failing at the one thing I’m supposed to be doing—being her mom—and the sadness feels heavy in my chest most of the day.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened twice this week. Yesterday I finally got her down for a nap, sat on the couch to pump, and just started sobbing. Nothing new had gone wrong; I just felt overwhelmed and hopeless. The tears come fast and hard, then leave me feeling empty and even more exhausted.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

A couple of times… just brief flashes. Like, I’ll be staring at the bottle warmer at three a.m. and think, “What if I just kept my hand on it?”—but I pull away right away and feel horrified I even had the idea. I don’t want to die; mostly I just want the anxious knot to stop. I haven’t told anyone because it scares me to say it out loud.

You've shared how the joy and anticipation you once felt has slipped away since your baby arrived, replaced by a heavy, gray sadness that lingers most of the day and night. Daily tasks feel overwhelming, laughter is fleeting or hollow, and anxious thoughts about your baby's safety race through your mind even when all is well. You described sudden tearfulness, panicky moments, exhausting guilt, and brief, frightening thoughts of self-harm that you quickly push away.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only a brief, hollow laugh and states "nothing feels very funny these days," matching "Definitely not so much now".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes loss of anticipatory joy ("flat," "isn't there anymore") matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily intrusive worries and physical anxiety symptoms despite no real danger, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two clear panic-like episodes this week with physical symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart, breathlessness) and anticipatory dread, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, inability to manage routine tasks, and feeling like "drowning" and "can't breathe," matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to persistent anxious thoughts, broken 3-hour total sleep, which aligns with 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "pretty much every day" and "most of the day," matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying twice this week, describing sudden overwhelming sobs followed by emptiness—semantically aligns with "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes brief, unwanted self-harm thoughts recurring a couple of times, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26 places you well above the EPDS threshold for probable major depression. You endorsed core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most days, markedly diminished interest, self-reproach, fatigue, sleep disruption beyond infant demands, and recurrent passive suicidal thoughts. <quote>I lie down exhausted but my head keeps spinning</quote> illustrates psychomotor agitation and insomnia; <quote>I feel like I'm failing at the one thing I'm supposed to be doing</quote> highlights inappropriate guilt. Combined with <sym>panic symptoms</sym> and <sym>intrusive worries</sym>, presentation suggests comorbid anxiety. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary-care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> to review mood, safety, and treatment options
2. Call the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (US) or your local emergency number if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe
3. Remove or secure items you might use for self-harm; share your thoughts with a trusted adult who can stay with you tonight
4. Consider starting evidence-based treatment-<med>CBT</med> or interpersonal therapy and/or medication compatible with breastfeeding-under physician guidance
5. Enlist practical help: partner, family, or postpartum doula for night feeds, meals, and household tasks so you can rest
6. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or five-minute grounding exercises when panic rises; keep lights dim and phone notes with affirmations nearby
7. Schedule pediatric or mother-baby follow-up within one week to monitor bonding, infant feeding, and your ongoing mood
8. Re-screen with EPDS in two weeks to track response to interventions
9. Maintain hydration, nutritious snacks, and brief outdoor daylight walks when safe; small, achievable steps support recovery
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant <12 mo)  
Date: ___

Presenting symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia (minimal pleasure from previously enjoyable activities)  
- Daily anxiety, intrusive “what-if” worries, nocturnal panic episode  
- Pervasive self-blame/guilt re infant care  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance difficulties not solely attributable to infant demands  
- Overwhelm, “drowning” in routine tasks, poor coping efficacy  
- Passive self-harm ideation (fleeting urge to burn self on bottle-warmer) without intent or plan  

Pattern summary  
Responses consistent across all 10 EPDS items; highest endorsement on sadness, anxiety, guilt, and self-harm items (score ≥12 likely). Functional impact evident in home management, infant care confidence, and nocturnal rest.

Screening significance / risk flags  
- Probable major depressive symptoms with comorbid anxiety  
- Passive suicidal ideation present → acute safety concern  
- Impaired maternal–infant bonding suggested by guilt and emotional flatness  

Next steps documented  
- Discuss immediate safety plan, supports, removal of lethal means  
- Recommend expedited psychiatric evaluation for diagnosis and treatment planning  
- Provide 24/7 crisis resources (988 / maternal MH hotline)
